evidence: Cic. Brut. 301: memoria tanta quantam in nūllō cognōvisse mē arbitror
terms.comment: A good memory: memoria bona (Cic. Att. 8.4.2); of the person, bonae memoriae esse (Petr. 66.1), bonā memoriā esse (Traupman 344) or memoriā vigēre (Aug. Conf. 1.20.31). From memory: ex memoriā (Cic. Cat. 3.13, Lewis & Short); to commit to memory, memoriae mandāre (Traupman 344; see learn by heart).

phrases.latin: ingeniī signum in parvīs praecipuum memoria est. ejus duplex virtūs, facile percipere et fidēliter continēre
phrases.english: in small children the chief sign of ability is memory, and its virtue is twofold: to take things in easily and to keep them faithfully

phrases.latin: initia litterārum sōlā memoriā cōnstant, quae nōn modo jam est in parvīs sed tum etiam tenācissima est
phrases.english: the first steps in learning rest on memory alone, which small children not only have already but have at its most retentive

phrases.latin: tamen quid habuistis in cēnā? — dīcam, sī potuerō; nam tam bonae memoriae sum, ut frequenter nōmen meum oblīvīscar
phrases.english: Still, what did you have for dinner? — I’ll tell you if I can; my memory is so good that I often forget my own name.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 344, checked against the searchable text of the book (9 November 2026).

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
